title: Estimating the bioavailability of a dose

segs.text: Module seven A, objective four. Estimating the bioavailability of a dose. Clearance, Cl, is the volume of plasma cleared of drug per hour, and it ties a dose to its area under the curve, A U C: the amount that reached the blood equals clearance times the area. For an I V dose that amount is the whole dose, and for an oral dose it is F, the fraction absorbed, times the dose. In one person clearance is the same for both routes, so dividing one line by the other cancels it and leaves F abs equals A U C p o over A U C I V, times D I V over D p o. She said, it doesn't matter which approach you use.

card.m: amount reaching the blood = Cl × AUC

segs.text: Because the area is the amount in the blood over clearance, three behaviors follow. With linear kinetics the area is proportional to the dose, so half the dose gives half the area. A higher clearance at the same dose gives a smaller area, because the drug is removed faster, but F does not change, because F is about how much entered. A lower F means less of the oral dose entered, so the oral area is smaller at the same clearance.

card.m: linear: AUC proportional to dose; ½ dose → ½ AUC
Cl higher → AUC smaller; F unchanged

segs.text: When a stem gives only the oral area, the I V area is built from clearance. For a one compartment drug clearance is k times V D, the elimination rate constant times the volume of distribution, and k is zero point six nine three over the half life. So A U C I V equals D I V over k times V D, and a half life and a volume are enough. Milligrams over liters per hour gives milligram hours per liter, the unit of an area. This is the Module four line, Cl T equals F D zero over A U C, with F equal to one.

Her in class question one asks the F of a five hundred milligram oral tablet with an area of seventy milligram hours per liter, and the area after a two hundred fifty milligram I V bolus. The same volunteer's five hundred milligram I V bolus had a half life of three hours and a V D of twenty five liters but no area, so the I V area comes from clearance. The doses are equal, so F is the area ratio, zero point eight zero eight five, about eighty one percent, and the clearance route gives the same. Half the I V dose gives half the area, forty three point two nine milligram hours per liter, because the kinetics are linear.

card.m: IV: D<sub>IV</sub> = 500 mg, t<sub>½</sub> = 3 hr, V<sub>D</sub> = 25 L

segs.text: Question three gives the I V curve itself: after a five hundred milligram bolus, the plasma concentration, C p, equals fifty e to the minus zero point two t. Matching the I V bolus line, C zero is fifty milligrams per liter and k is zero point two per hour, so V D is ten liters and clearance two liters per hour. The I V area is two hundred fifty milligram hours per liter, so a five hundred milligram tablet with an area of one hundred eighty eight milligram hours per liter has an F of zero point seven five two, seventy five percent.

card.m: V<sub>D</sub> = {{frac:500 mg|50 mg/L}} = 10 L; Cl = 0.2 hr<sup>−1</sup> × 10 L = 2 L/hr

segs.text: Turned around, F gives the oral dose that matches an I V dose. Same extent means equal areas, and with the same clearance equal areas mean the same amount reached the blood, so F times the oral dose equals the I V dose. So the oral dose is the I V dose divided by F. F is underneath, so the lower F is, the larger the oral dose, and an F of one makes the two doses equal. She said, You expect that you're gonna have a larger, um, P O dose, right?

card.m: F lower → D<sub>po</sub> larger; F = 1 → D<sub>po</sub> = D<sub>IV</sub>

segs.text: Her first example took the tablet from her practice problem, with an F of zero point five five, and asked the oral dose equivalent to one hundred milligrams I V. It is about one hundred eighty two milligrams, almost twice the I V dose, because almost half of each oral dose is lost. That number is then rounded to a dose that makes sense. She said, We might round it to two hundred if there's a one seventy five or something that makes sense as opposed to one eighty one.

card.m: ≈ 200 mg, a dose that makes sense

segs.text: Question two: ciprofloxacin has an oral immediate release F of seventy percent, and the oral dose with the same extent as a four hundred milligram I V bolus is asked. Four hundred milligrams over zero point seven zero is five hundred seventy one point four three milligrams, not a real tablet, since the strengths she looked up were two hundred fifty and five hundred. She wrote five hundred seventy five, six hundred or five hundred seventy beside it, and when a stem asks for the nearest five, five hundred seventy is the answer, as in her review. The rounding instruction in the stem comes first, and a tablet strength that exists is used only when the stem gives no rounding instruction.

Her poll is the model item: a five hundred milligram tablet with an area of one hundred fifteen milligram hours per liter, against a four hundred milligram I V bolus with one hundred thirty two. With the I V area underneath and the I V dose on top, F is zero point six nine seven, seventy percent. Inverting the dose ratio gives one point zero eight nine, and the area ratio alone zero point eight seven one; both are wrong. When a stem has two different doses, as in her Exam two review, F uses the oral dose that made the oral area, five hundred milligrams, and the equivalent oral dose is the replaced I V dose, nine hundred milligrams, divided by F: twelve hundred milligrams.

card.m: her review: AUC<sub>IV</sub> for 500 mg = {{frac:500 mg|1.86 L/hr}} = 268.8 (mg/L)hr; F = {{frac:202|268.8}} = 0.75
IV dose replaced 900 mg: {{frac:900 mg|0.75}} = 1200 mg
